paragraphs: The core problem is that a service provider's crew, equipment pool, and certification roster are shared resources deployed across many separate client relationships, while the reporting, terminology, and often the acceptance criteria for each of those relationships need to stay distinct. A platform built around a single asset hierarchy handles this badly — either every client's data gets visually mixed together, or the company ends up running a separate instance or spreadsheet per client, which defeats the purpose of having a system of record at all. The workable model keeps one underlying resource pool of technicians, equipment, and certifications, while partitioning report templates, terminology sets, and client-facing structure per contract.

Crew and certification availability is the second layer of the same problem. A scheduler needs visibility across every active client commitment simultaneously to answer a basic question — is a technician with current [PAUT](/ndt-methods) certification and no conflicting assignment available for a job starting Thursday — without that visibility leaking client-specific job details across contracts that shouldn't see each other. This is different from what an [owner-operator's asset integrity platform](/asset-integrity-management-software) needs to solve, because an owner-operator is scheduling against its own assets, not arbitrating capacity across a portfolio of unrelated client commitments.

Billing and scope boundaries follow the same logic. When the same technician logs time against a fabrication inspection for one client in the morning and a refinery turnaround job for another client that afternoon, the system needs those hours, that equipment usage, and that report output to stay attributable to the correct contract without manual reconciliation after the fact — otherwise scope creep between contracts becomes a billing dispute waiting to happen rather than something the software prevented by design. [ERP integration](/erp) on the billing and scheduling side is often what closes this gap for service providers running enough concurrent contracts that spreadsheet reconciliation stops being viable.

None of this requires a different platform per client relationship — it requires the underlying system to treat client and contract as first-class fields that every report template, every schedule entry, and every billing record inherits automatically, rather than something a project manager has to manually enforce by discipline and habit across dozens of concurrent jobs.

Terminology mapping is a smaller but constant friction point: one client calls a component grouping a circuit, another calls the same grouping a zone, and a third uses the numbering scheme from their own CMMS rather than any inspection-specific convention. A platform that hardcodes one naming convention forces the inspection company to either retrain technicians per client or manually relabel every report before it goes out, neither of which is where a service provider's differentiation should be spent.

answer: OSHA's Process Safety Management standard requires a documented mechanical integrity program, and the audit trail an inspector actually checks is the closed loop from inspection finding to fitness-for-service or RBI disposition to verified deficiency correction. Asset integrity software supports that element by keeping those three records — finding, disposition, correction — linked to the same equipment record instead of scattered across separate systems.
expansion: 29 CFR 1910.119(j) requires inspection and testing procedures that follow recognized and generally accepted good engineering practice, and it requires that deficiencies outside acceptable limits get corrected before further use, or in a safe and timely manner otherwise. In an audit, that translates into a specific evidence chain an inspector will pull: the inspection record that found the deficiency, the engineering evaluation — often an [API 579 fitness-for-service assessment](/consulting/fitness-for-service-api-579) — that determined whether the equipment could keep running and under what conditions, and the closure record proving the deficiency was actually corrected, not just logged. When those three pieces live in three different systems, or worse, in email threads and spreadsheets, reconstructing that chain for an audit becomes a manual research project instead of a query.
source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119 (Process Safety Management)

sections.heading: Mechanical integrity under OSHA PSM: closing the loop from finding to correction
paragraphs: The mechanical integrity element of a PSM program is judged less on whether inspections happened and more on whether findings that fell outside acceptable limits were tracked to actual resolution. A wall-thickness reading below the retirement limit, a crack indication exceeding acceptance criteria — these need a documented disposition path: a fitness-for-service evaluation determining whether the component can run as-is, needs a rerate, or requires repair, followed by a verified correction if repair or replacement was the outcome. Software support for this means the deficiency record doesn't close itself when the inspection report is filed; it stays open until the disposition and, where applicable, the corrective action are both documented against it.

The connection to RBI matters here too: a deficiency that gets corrected should also update the [risk-based inspection interval](/consulting/rbi-program-design) for that circuit going forward, because the corrective action changes the actual condition the next interval calculation should be based on. Treating the PSM correction record and the RBI risk model as separate, unconnected systems means the interval schedule keeps running on outdated assumptions even after the underlying problem was fixed.

This is a narrower slice of what a full mechanical integrity program covers — inspector qualification, equipment-specific inspection frequency, and documentation retention are all part of 1910.119(j) as well. [The dedicated treatment of mechanical integrity program requirements](/mechanical-integrity-software) covers that fuller scope; the point here is specifically how the finding-to-disposition-to-correction chain has to work as a connected record, not a set of independent filings, for the audit trail to hold up.

answer: NDT inspection software and asset integrity management software overlap but cover different scope: NDT software is built around capturing and reporting individual inspection results — UT readings, RT film, PAUT scans — while asset integrity software sits a layer above, aggregating those results against an asset's full history to drive fitness-for-service and RBI decisions facility-wide.
expansion: That distinction matters when evaluating either category. The capabilities that decide an NDT software purchase — offline field capture, [method-specific data formats and calibration tracking](/ndt-methods), report generation against inspection code templates — are about capturing and reporting a single inspection correctly. [Asset integrity management software](/asset-integrity-management-software) assumes that inspection data already exists and is trustworthy, then builds on top of it: rolling individual readings into a circuit-level corrosion rate, feeding that rate into an RBI risk score, and tracking fitness-for-service disposition once a finding crosses an acceptance limit. A service provider running inspections across multiple clients is usually closer to [inspection management software](/inspection-management-software) territory; an owner-operator managing its own equipment over decades typically needs both, usually as connected systems rather than one product doing everything.
source: API 510 / API 570 / API 653 Inspection Codes

sections.heading: Where the scope boundary actually falls
paragraphs: The cleanest way to draw the line is by what happens to a reading after capture: if the software's job ends at a correct, code-compliant inspection report, that's NDT inspection software; if it continues on to compare the new reading against prior cycles and update a circuit's risk category, that's [asset integrity management software](/asset-integrity-management-software) territory, even when both functions live in the same platform.

answer: Atlantis NDT ERP modules are not independent apps bolted together — certification tracking, calibration management, work orders and reporting share one data model, so a technician's current certification status, the calibration state of the instrument they are assigned, and the project they are dispatched to are always read from the same underlying record rather than three systems that can silently drift apart.
expansion: A generic ERP treats "who is certified," "what is calibrated" and "what job is scheduled" as three unrelated tables, which is exactly how a decertified technician gets dispatched with an overdue instrument on a live work order — nobody's fault, just three systems that never talked to each other. Atlantis configures these as one connected model: a work order cannot be assigned to a technician whose certification for that method has lapsed, and a technician cannot be paired with an instrument outside its calibration window. The modules below are the visible surface of that shared model, not separate products.
source: ISO 9712 (personnel certification) and ISO 17025 (calibration) as the two schemes the module interdependency is built around

sections.heading: How the modules actually interlock
paragraphs: Certification tracking is the gate the other modules read from, not a standalone register. When a work order module schedules a UT inspection, it checks the assigned technician's current UT certification level and expiry against SNT-TC-1A or ISO 9712 before the job confirms — the same check a client audit performs manually, done automatically at dispatch time instead of discovered after the fact.

Calibration management works the same way against equipment. An instrument due for recalibration is flagged in the calibration module, and that flag is visible to the work-order module before a crew is assigned it for a field job — not as a separate report someone has to remember to cross-check.

Reporting closes the loop: every report the system generates carries the technician's certification state and the instrument's calibration state as they stood at the moment of inspection, not as they stand today. That distinction is what a client audit actually asks for — a snapshot, not a current status.

facets.q: Can we run only the modules we need, not the full platform?
facets.a: Yes — modules are configured to what the business actually runs; a company doing only field inspection work does not need the ERP's manufacturing-adjacent modules turned on. The interlocking checks (certification-gates-dispatch, calibration-gates-assignment) apply to whichever modules are active.

facets.q: What happens if a technician's certification lapses mid-project?
facets.a: The work-order module blocks new assignments to that technician for the affected method the moment the certification-tracking module marks it expired; work already dispatched is flagged for review rather than silently continuing.

facets.q: Does adding a module require re-entering existing data?
facets.a: No — modules read from the same technician, equipment and project records already in the system; turning on a new module extends what those records can do rather than duplicating them.

answer: RAGAGEP compliance is usually asserted in an MI programme, not documented — a procedure references API 510 or API 653 in general, but nothing in the record shows which specific clause governed a specific inspection decision on a specific piece of equipment. Atlantis ties the RAGAGEP citation to the equipment class and the finding, not to the programme as a whole.
expansion: An auditor testing OSHA PSM mechanical integrity does not accept "we follow API codes" as an answer to "why was this interval chosen" — they want the specific clause. A pressure vessel's inspection interval traces to a specific paragraph in API 510; a storage tank's traces to a specific paragraph in API 653; a piping circuit's traces to API 570. When those citations live only in an engineer's head or a procedure document nobody re-reads, the finding record can't reproduce the reasoning, and that gap — not the interval itself — is what generates the audit finding. Atlantis stores the governing clause as an attribute of the equipment class, so every interval decision it generates carries its own citation automatically.
source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(j) — mechanical integrity, RAGAGEP requirement

sections.heading: Citing the specific practice, not the programme
paragraphs: Every equipment class in the system carries its governing RAGAGEP reference as data, not as a note in a separate procedure binder: pressure vessels cite API 510, storage tanks cite API 653, piping circuits cite API 570, and each is scoped to the specific clause an interval decision relies on.

When an interval or a repair decision is generated, the citation travels with it into the record — so six months later, when an auditor asks why a specific tank got a specific interval, the answer is retrievable in seconds rather than reconstructed from memory.

answer: Under ASNT SNT-TC-1A, it is the employer's written practice — not ASNT itself — that sets the training hours, experience hours, and passing score a technician must meet before that employer can certify them. ISO 9712 candidates test instead through an accredited third-party certification body, which is why the two schemes produce credentials with different portability for the same UT or RT qualification.
expansion: That distinction matters more in Abu Dhabi than in most markets because so much of the workforce rotates between ADNOC group companies, EPC main contractors, and inspection subcontractors across the same brownfield turnaround. A Level II certified under one employer's written practice is not automatically qualified to sign reports for a different employer — the receiving employer's Level III has to review the credential against its own written practice and either accept it or require supplemental examination. Recertification intervals under SNT-TC-1A are commonly no longer than five years for most methods, with the written practice itself specifying whether renewal means a full re-examination or a documented review of continued satisfactory performance plus a current vision test. ISO 9712 runs on its own five-year cycle through the certification body, with a fresh examination typically required at the second renewal. Neither scheme treats the original certificate as a lifetime credential; currency has to be actively maintained.
source: ASNT SNT-TC-1A

sections.heading: The written practice: the document your certification actually rests on
paragraphs: Most candidates assume ASNT itself issues and polices their certification. Under SNT-TC-1A it doesn't — ASNT publishes a recommended practice, complete with suggested minimum training-hour and experience-hour tables by method and level, but it is each employer's own written practice, approved and signed by a qualified Level III, that turns that recommendation into an enforceable requirement. A written practice specifies, method by method and level by level, the minimum classroom hours, the minimum documented on-the-job experience hours, the content and passing score of the general, specific and practical examinations, how often near-vision acuity and colour-contrast are retested, and the conditions under which a certification can be suspended or revoked. Two technicians who both hold an 'ASNT Level II UT' certificate issued in Abu Dhabi may have met genuinely different real requirements, because the two employers' written practices differ — one company's minimum experience hours for UT Level II can run well above SNT-TC-1A's suggested minimum while another sticks to the floor, and a receiving employer is entitled to ask which written practice a candidate actually certified against before accepting the credential at face value. ISO 9712 sidesteps this variability by removing the employer from the certifying role entirely.

For corporate cohorts in Abu Dhabi, Atlantis works from the client's existing written practice wherever one is already in force, and helps draft or update one — aligned to the SNT-TC-1A recommended structure and cross-checked against ISO 9712 where a client runs both schemes side by side — for companies building an inspection function for the first time, which describes a fair number of newer fabrication yards, marine contractors and EPC subcontractors entering this market as ADNOC's supplier base expands. A written practice that is silent on a method the crew actually performs, that predates a code revision the crew is now expected to work to, or that has gone years without a Level III signature refreshing it, is one of the first documents a client's QA auditor or an ADNOC vendor-qualification reviewer asks to see — independent of whether the individual technicians on the crew are demonstrably competent at the bench. Getting that document right before a cohort starts, rather than retrofitting it afterward, is usually the difference between an audit that takes an afternoon and one that reopens every certificate on the crew list. See [how ASNT certification works](/asnt-certification) for more on how the written practice sits alongside the codes it draws from.

sections.heading: Recertification, reverification, and staying current
paragraphs: A certificate earned once is not a certificate held forever, and the distinction between recertification and reverification trips up more technicians than the original exam does. Reverification applies while a technician's employment and job performance are continuous: no gap in service, a current vision and colour-contrast test, and evidence of ongoing satisfactory performance are usually enough to keep the certification active without sitting a new exam. Recertification applies at the written practice's stated interval — commonly set at no more than five years for most methods under SNT-TC-1A, though some employers set a shorter interval for higher-consequence methods like radiography — and depending on the employer's own document, it can mean either a full re-examination or a documented performance review plus a current vision test. Let the interval lapse without either path completed, and most written practices treat the technician as starting over rather than simply renewing, which on a multi-year Ruwais turnaround schedule — where a technician might rotate between two or three different scopes of work over several years — is a genuinely common and avoidable finding on a personnel-file audit.

ISO 9712 runs its own five-year cycle through the accredited certification body rather than the employer, with a fresh practical and written examination typically required at the second renewal regardless of how strong the technician's job performance has been in the interim — a meaningful difference for anyone weighing SNT-TC-1A against ISO 9712 for a career that might move between Gulf markets. Neither clock transfers automatically to the other scheme: a technician moving from an SNT-TC-1A employer in Abu Dhabi into a market that runs on ISO 9712, or vice versa, has to sit that scheme's own qualifying examination, prior certification history notwithstanding, and building that transition time into a project timeline avoids a technician showing up on-site with a certificate the new contract doesn't actually recognise. For a corporate client running several hundred certifications across rotating shift crews, tracking renewal dates on a spreadsheet is exactly where dates get missed; Atlantis's [NDT ERP](/erp) tracks certification expiry alongside equipment calibration due dates so a recertification gap surfaces as a scheduling flag weeks in advance, before it turns into an audit finding on a live job.

sections.heading: Offshore, marine, and storage-tank inspection load specific to Abu Dhabi
paragraphs: Abu Dhabi's inspection demand isn't only onshore. ADNOC Offshore operates producing fields — Upper Zakum among the largest offshore oil accumulations anywhere, alongside Umm Shaif, Lower Zakum, Satah, and the newer artificial-island production complexes built out over the last decade — developed in long-running joint ventures with international operators, and every platform, riser and subsea pipeline in that system runs on an inspection interval that has to be met by certified personnel working topside, in the splash zone, or through diver- or ROV-deployed tooling. That pulls a heavier local weighting toward UT wall-thickness and corrosion mapping on risers and topside piping, MT and magnetic-particle work on structural welds exposed to fatigue loading from wave and wind action, and eddy current and ACFM for coating-covered welds where surface preparation for conventional MT or PT isn't practical offshore — a method mix that differs meaningfully from a purely onshore refining or pipeline crew's emphasis. Technicians who train only against onshore specimens sometimes struggle with the access constraints and surface conditions that offshore and splash-zone work actually present, which is a gap corporate cohorts serving marine and offshore clients specifically ask us to close in the practical block.

Ruwais and the surrounding terminal network also carry a large aboveground storage tank population, and tank floor and shell inspection — UT thickness grids, magnetic flux leakage floor scanning, and vacuum-box testing of shell welds — is scheduled, recurring work rather than a one-off project, which keeps UT, MT and PT technicians in continuous local demand independent of new-build activity. That inspection data feeds directly into asset-integrity decisions: a UT reading that shows a tank floor thinning toward a code limit is the trigger for a fitness-for-service evaluation, and a pattern of readings across a tank farm over successive inspection cycles is what a [risk-based inspection program](/consulting/rbi-program-design) uses to set the next interval rather than defaulting to a fixed code-minimum schedule. Atlantis's method-level training for the technicians generating those readings sits directly upstream of that asset-integrity consulting work — the same reason we ask a corporate client what their inspection data actually feeds into, and who reviews it, before designing the training plan, rather than treating the training booking as a standalone exercise disconnected from what the readings are eventually used for.

sections.heading: What a client or vendor-qualification audit actually checks in a technician's file
paragraphs: A valid certificate is necessary but not sufficient. An ADNOC vendor-prequalification review or a client's periodic QA audit typically pulls a sample of personnel files and traces a full chain: the certificate itself, a vision and colour-contrast test dated within the required interval, a training-hours record, an experience log signed off by a supervising Level III, the examination records behind the certificate, and — for the file to actually hold up under scrutiny — evidence that the written practice the technician certified against was itself signed by a currently-certified, qualified Level III rather than one whose own certification has since lapsed. A technician with an otherwise valid certificate can still fail that review if the supporting file is incomplete, if a signature is missing, or if the written practice behind it can't be produced on request — which in practice is a more common audit finding than an outright invalid certification. It is one of the reasons Atlantis hands a corporate client a structured qualification file for the whole cohort at the end of a programme — certificate, experience log, exam record and vision test bundled per technician — rather than a stack of individual certificates for the client's QA team to reassemble later.

UAE Emiratisation requirements add a second, workforce-composition layer to that same audit conversation. Private-sector Emiratisation quotas apply to companies above a defined size under UAE labour policy, with the required share of Emirati employment increasing year over year, and oil & gas contractors renewing or expanding their inspection workforce increasingly need a documented, staged path that takes UAE national candidates from Level I through Level II inside their own written practice — not only a hiring pipeline of already-certified expatriate technicians. That reframes the training conversation for a number of Abu Dhabi employers: less a one-off exam-prep booking and more a standing internal pipeline, with cohort scheduling built around incumbent staff development and mentored on-the-job hours rather than a single intake of outside hires. Corporate training built around that kind of staged progression is a different design problem from public individual enrolment, and it's usually worth a short scoping call before committing to a cohort structure — [talk it through](/contact).

facets.q: What is a written practice, and why does it matter more than the ASNT certificate itself?
facets.a: A written practice is the employer's own document — not an ASNT-issued standard — that sets the actual training hours, experience hours, exam content and passing marks a technician must meet under SNT-TC-1A, and it has to be signed by a qualified Level III to be valid. Two 'Level II UT' certificates from two different Abu Dhabi employers can represent genuinely different real requirements, because each is measured against its own employer's written practice rather than a single central bar, which is exactly what a receiving employer or auditor checks before accepting one at face value.

facets.q: How often does an NDT technician need to recertify in Abu Dhabi?
facets.a: Under SNT-TC-1A, recertification intervals are set by the employer's written practice and commonly run no longer than five years for most methods, with the interim period covered by reverification — continuous employment, satisfactory job performance and a current vision and colour-contrast test rather than a full new examination. ISO 9712 runs its own five-year cycle through the accredited certification body instead of the employer, with a fresh practical and written examination typically required at the second renewal regardless of demonstrated job performance in between.

facets.q: Does offshore work around Abu Dhabi call for different NDT training than onshore refining work?
facets.a: Yes, in emphasis rather than in the base method set. Offshore platforms and subsea pipelines around fields like Upper Zakum and Umm Shaif weight UT corrosion mapping, structural MT under fatigue loading, and coating-tolerant methods like ACFM and eddy current more heavily, alongside the access and surface-condition challenges of splash-zone and topside work. Onshore Ruwais refining work weights phased-array UT on welds, thickness monitoring on process piping, and tank floor and shell inspection more heavily — the practical training block should reflect whichever environment the crew actually works in.

facets.q: Will a certification I earned with one Abu Dhabi employer be accepted by my next employer?
facets.a: Not automatically. A receiving employer's Level III has to review the credential against that employer's own written practice and can accept it as-is, require supplemental training, or require re-examination before certifying you under their document — the certificate itself doesn't obligate them to accept it unchanged. ISO 9712 credentials, issued by an accredited third-party certification body rather than by an individual employer, tend to travel more predictably between employers for exactly this reason, which is one factor worth weighing when choosing a certification route.

facets.q: Do UAE Emiratisation requirements change how a corporate NDT training cohort is structured?
facets.a: For companies above the size threshold UAE Emiratisation quotas apply to, yes — training increasingly has to build a staged Level I-to-Level II pipeline for UAE national candidates inside the employer's written practice, with documented mentored hours, rather than relying only on already-certified expatriate hires. That changes cohort scheduling from a single exam-prep intake into an ongoing internal programme run alongside normal crew rotations, which is a different design conversation than a straightforward corporate booking and usually needs to be scoped separately.

answer: A Dallas–Fort Worth written practice under SNT-TC-1A lays out, method by method, the minimum training hours, the on-the-job experience hours, and the general, specific and practical examinations a candidate must clear before an employer certifies them — commonly graded around 70% on the general and specific exams and higher on the practical — backed by an annual vision exam and a recertification interval capped at five years.
expansion: Contract-facing Dallas–Fort Worth work turns on a document most candidates never see before they need it: the written practice that sets, per method and level, the training hours, the OJT experience hours, and the general, specific and practical exam trio an employer certifies against, backed by an annual vision exam and a recertification interval SNT-TC-1A caps at five years. Corporate cohorts qualify a crew against that document on the employer's own equipment and specimens, producing one internally consistent record instead of certifications collected from different providers over different years — which is exactly what a client audit compares. A hiring employer or auditor checks the written-practice edition in force at exam time, hour logs against timesheets, and the designation behind whoever signed the qualification, not the card itself. Nuclear-adjacent inspection near Fort Worth, at a site like Comanche Peak, layers a further nuclear QA programme on top of that baseline.
source: ASNT SNT-TC-1A

sections.heading: Inside the written practice: what SNT-TC-1A actually specifies
paragraphs: The written practice a Dallas–Fort Worth employer certifies against is not a policy memo — it is a working technical document that sets, method by method and level by level, the minimum recommended training hours, the on-the-job experience hours that run alongside them, and the structure of the qualifying examinations. SNT-TC-1A's own recommended-minimum-hours tables set penetrant and magnetic particle classroom hours well below ultrasonic and radiographic testing at both Level I and Level II, reflecting how much longer it takes to build competence in a technique that requires interpreting a waveform or a film rather than reading a visible indication. The qualifying exam itself is really three exams: a general exam on the method's underlying principles, a specific exam tied to the employer's own procedures and equipment, and a practical exam demonstrating the technique on real or reference specimens — conventionally graded around a 70% pass on the general and specific portions and a higher bar on the practical, since a marginal pass on hands-on technique is a marginal pass on the thing the certification is actually meant to guarantee.

Two provisions in the written practice run on their own clock, independent of the certification's validity period. An annual near-vision acuity test — reading a Jaeger 1 equivalent at roughly twelve inches, natural or corrected — and a colour-contrast discrimination check where the method calls for it, both have to stay current or the certification is suspended regardless of how much time is left on the five-year cycle. Recertification itself, under SNT-TC-1A, is conventionally due at intervals not exceeding five years and is contingent on continued satisfactory job performance being on file, not automatic renewal — which is one reason the [written practice](/standards) an employer adopts matters more, in an audit, than any individual certificate it produces.

The written practice also carries provisions for suspension, probation and revocation that rarely come up until they matter — a certification can be suspended for cause (a documented performance failure, an expired vision exam, evidence the individual worked outside their qualified method or level) independent of the five-year clock, and reinstatement typically requires demonstrating the deficiency has been corrected rather than simply waiting it out. Record retention is set by the same document: most Dallas–Fort Worth written practices keep the qualification file — exam results, hour logs, vision exam history — on file for the life of the certification plus at least one additional cycle, precisely so that record exists when a client audit or a new employer asks for it years later rather than at the moment of hire.

sections.heading: How the Level I to Level III path actually plays out
paragraphs: Moving from Level I to Level II in a given method is not a second training course from zero — a Level I logs additional documented on-the-job hours in that method under a certified Level II or III, and once the hour threshold and time-in-grade are met, sits the specific and practical portion of the Level II exam in that method alone. Multi-method tracks work the same way per method rather than in aggregate: classroom training for ultrasonic and radiographic testing can be scheduled together, but the OJT hours for each bank on separate clocks, so a Dallas–Fort Worth technician chasing UT and RT Level II at the same time finishes on whichever method's hours accumulate slower, not the faster.

Level III is where the qualifying basis changes shape rather than just growing longer. SNT-TC-1A recognises several accepted combinations of formal education and documented NDT experience for Level III — a four-year engineering or science degree paired with a shorter experience requirement, an associate degree with more, or no post-secondary credential at all paired with a longer one — and a fair number of Dallas–Fort Worth employers reference the centralized [ASNT NDT Level III Certification Program](/asnt-certification) rather than qualifying a Level III entirely in-house, because that programme's basic, method and specific examinations are administered independently of any one employer and stay portable if the individual later moves to a different company.

sections.heading: Corporate cohorts vs individual enrolment: what actually differs beyond where training happens
paragraphs: The difference is not only travel and location. A corporate cohort is built to leave the employer holding a defensible written practice, not just a room of trained people — every candidate tests against the same procedure set, on the same specimens, under the same proctor, so the grading is internally consistent across the crew. That consistency is exactly what a client audit is checking for when several technicians on one job are carrying certifications issued by different providers in different years under different written practices. Cohorts are usually scheduled around a plant's outage or turnaround calendar rather than a fixed course date, and the practical portion draws on the facility's own welds, castings or machined parts, so the qualification maps onto the scope of work the crew will actually be assigned rather than a generic reference set.

Individual enrolment runs the opposite way out of necessity. A single candidate typically qualifies against a portable written practice and a standard specimen set, which suits someone moving between employers or working through a contract-inspection or staffing house rather than certifying for one plant's use. That portability is a starting point, not a guarantee — an incoming Level II is still checked against the receiving employer's own written practice and specific exam before being put on that facility's work. A Dallas–Fort Worth operator standing up a certification programme without a Level III on staff typically pairs the corporate route with an [outsourced designated Level III of record](/consulting/asnt-level-iii-consulting-services) so the written practice itself, not just the trained crew, survives the engagement.

The demand behind those corporate bookings is concrete rather than abstract. Lockheed Martin runs F-35 Lightning II final assembly at its Fort Worth plant, work qualified under NAS 410 and EN 4179 rather than SNT-TC-1A; Bell, headquartered in Fort Worth, builds helicopters under the same aerospace framework; and Energy Transfer, headquartered in Dallas, operates pipeline and midstream assets qualified under SNT-TC-1A with acceptance to API 1104 and the ASME B31 series. Add the structural steel fabrication shops serving both industries and North Texas construction generally, and a single Dallas–Fort Worth region ends up running two largely separate certification economies side by side — which is exactly why a corporate cohort's written practice has to be built for the specific code stack the crew will be tested against, not a generic multi-industry template.

sections.heading: What a client audit or hiring employer actually checks before accepting a certification
paragraphs: A wallet card is not what gets inspected. An auditor working a Dallas–Fort Worth EPC's or operator's supplier quality review pulls the qualification record behind it and checks several things at once: which edition of the written practice was in force on the exam date, whether the vision exam is current inside its own required window rather than merely inside the certification's five-year cycle, whether the documented OJT hours reconcile against timesheets or project records instead of resting on self-attestation, and whether the Level III — or, on aerospace work, the Responsible Level 3 — who approved the qualification was themselves properly designated, with a dated authorization on file. A gap in continuous certification, where someone let a cycle lapse before renewing, can trigger a requirement to re-sit the exam rather than simply catch up on paperwork, and different employers set that gap tolerance differently inside their own [written practice](/glossary).

Nuclear-adjacent work adds a layer that's easy to miss from outside the industry. Comanche Peak Nuclear Power Plant, roughly sixty miles southwest of Fort Worth near Glen Rose, performs in-service inspection under ASME Section XI — a programme that leans heavily on manual and automated ultrasonic testing for reactor coolant system welds and piping, with surface methods covering weld overlay and support structure — and that inspection work typically layers a 10 CFR Part 50 Appendix B nuclear quality-assurance programme on top of the SNT-TC-1A or CP-189 qualification itself. A technician has to satisfy both the written practice and the site's own QA procedure before being accepted onto that work, a stricter combination than most refinery or midstream contracts in the region require.

Where the documentation gap is smaller — a lost training certificate rather than a missing hour log — many written practices allow the employer's own Level III to reconstruct the record from secondary evidence: project timesheets, procedure sign-off sheets, prior employer verification letters, or a sworn affidavit from the supervising Level II or III at the time. What a written practice will not accept is retroactively inventing hours that were never actually worked, and a Level III who signs off on a record they know is incomplete is putting their own designation at risk, not just the technician's certification. For a Dallas–Fort Worth crew moving between employers or contract houses over several years, keeping personal copies of exam results and hour logs — not just relying on the employer's file — is the difference between a fast requalification and starting over.

facets.q: What documents does an auditor actually ask to see, not just the certificate?
facets.a: The qualification record behind it: which written-practice edition governed the exam, the scored general, specific and practical exam results, the OJT hour log tied to timesheets or project records, and the current vision-exam certificate. A wallet card with a signature is not, on its own, evidence of anything — it summarizes a file the auditor expects to be able to pull.

facets.q: How often does an NDT certification actually need renewing in Texas?
facets.a: Texas does not license NDT technicians the way it licenses some trades — certification is an industry, not a state, requirement, governed by whichever written practice or independent scheme the contract names. Under SNT-TC-1A the interval is set by the employer's own written practice and conventionally runs no longer than five years, with the vision exam renewed on its own shorter cycle regardless.

facets.q: Does a Level II technician need a college degree?
facets.a: No. Employer-based Level I and Level II qualification under SNT-TC-1A runs on training hours and documented OJT experience, not formal education. A degree only enters the picture at Level III, where several accepted combinations of education and experience — more experience required with less schooling, less with more — set the qualifying basis.

facets.q: Can one Dallas–Fort Worth crew be qualified in several methods on the same schedule?
facets.a: Yes for the classroom portion — a cohort can sit ultrasonic and radiographic theory back to back in the same week. The on-the-job hours behind each method don't compress the same way, though, since they're logged separately under supervision in that specific method; a written practice can schedule the training close together without shortening the experience clock underneath it.

facets.q: Which method carries most of the inspection volume on nuclear in-service work near Fort Worth?
facets.a: Ultrasonic testing, by a wide margin — ASME Section XI in-service inspection relies on manual and automated UT for reactor coolant system welds, piping and vessel examinations, with surface methods such as magnetic particle and liquid penetrant covering accessible welds and supports. It's a different method mix than the radiography-heavy pipeline girth-weld work elsewhere in North Texas.

answer: A Level II certificate rests on three separate examinations: a general exam on the method's underlying physics and equipment, a specific exam on the employer's own procedures and product forms, and a practical exam demonstrating the technique on real specimens. SNT-TC-1A recommends passing grades of 70% general, 70% specific, and an 80% composite average across all three.
expansion: New Orleans sits at the foot of the River Parishes petrochemical corridor running upriver toward Baton Rouge, one of the densest concentrations of refining and chemical processing capacity in North America, and close to Port Fourchon, the onshore logistics base that services most Gulf of Mexico deepwater oil and gas production, along with the Louisiana Offshore Oil Port, the only US terminal able to receive fully loaded supertankers. The Port of New Orleans itself moves heavy steel, project cargo and fabricated modules that get examined before and after shipment. Layered on top of that industrial density is a coastal, hurricane-exposed, high-humidity environment that accelerates corrosion under insulation and atmospheric corrosion on external piping and tankage — which is why thickness survey frequency in this region often runs tighter than the code minimum rather than to it. A technician certifying here is certifying into that combination of asset density and corrosion severity, not into a generic Gulf Coast market.
source: ASNT SNT-TC-1A

sections.heading: What a compliant Written Practice actually documents
paragraphs: The Written Practice referenced throughout this page is not a policy statement — it is a detailed technical document, and understanding what it actually contains explains why an auditor asks for it before the certificate. A compliant Written Practice under SNT-TC-1A sets out, per method and per level: the education and experience prerequisites a candidate must hold before sitting for certification; the minimum classroom training hours; the structure and content of the general, specific and practical examinations, including minimum passing grades; the frequency of the near-vision acuity and color-contrast examination; the interval at which certification must be renewed and whether renewal requires reexamination or documented evidence of continued satisfactory performance; and the conditions under which a certification can be suspended, revoked or reinstated. It is signed by the employer's Level III, who carries responsibility for everything in it.

SNT-TC-1A is a recommended practice, not a mandatory standard, so an employer is free to adopt its recommended tables as written or to modify them — shortening a recertification interval, adding a method-specific practical exercise, raising a passing grade — provided the modification is documented and defensible. That flexibility is the entire point of the SNT-TC-1A model, and it is also why two Level II certificates issued by two different Gulf Coast employers, even in the same method, are not necessarily built to the same requirement. Companies without an in-house Level III typically engage an [outsourced Level III](/consulting/asnt-level-iii-consulting-services) to write and administer it, which does not change what the document has to contain. A client auditor reading the Written Practice is checking exactly that: not whether a certificate exists, but whether the document behind it holds up.

sections.heading: The three-part examination and what each part is actually checking
paragraphs: Every method-level certification under SNT-TC-1A rests on three separate examinations, and conflating them is a common misunderstanding among candidates preparing for a first Level II. The general examination tests the fundamentals of the method itself — the underlying physics, the equipment and its controls, standard terminology and reference procedures — content that does not change from one employer to the next and that maps onto the broader body of NDT [standards](/standards) referenced across every code stack an inspector works under. The specific examination tests the candidate against the employer's own written procedures: the equipment models actually in use, the product forms and material thicknesses actually examined, and the acceptance criteria the employer's contracts actually reference. The practical examination is a hands-on demonstration — calibrating the equipment, examining a real or representative specimen, interpreting the indication, and producing a report that would stand in a client's file. SNT-TC-1A recommends passing grades of 70% for the general and specific examinations and 80% for the practical, with an 80% composite average across all three; an employer's Written Practice can set a higher bar but rarely a lower one.

Recertification follows the same three-part logic on a longer interval. SNT-TC-1A leaves the exact renewal period to the employer's Written Practice but recommends it not exceed five years, and requires either reexamination or documented evidence of continued satisfactory performance in the method at renewal, on top of an annual near-vision acuity and color-contrast check that runs independently of the certification cycle itself. A technician whose eyesight fails that annual check is not qualified to interpret indications regardless of how recent the certificate is.

sections.heading: Where Louisiana's NDE demand actually concentrates
paragraphs: The industrial geography around New Orleans is not evenly spread, and a training programme built for this market benefits from following where the work actually sits rather than treating the whole Gulf Coast as one undifferentiated zone. Running north from New Orleans along the Mississippi River, the River Parishes — St. Charles, St. John the Baptist, St. James and neighbouring parishes — carry one of the densest concentrations of refining and petrochemical processing capacity in North America, all of it running scheduled turnarounds that pull heavily on ultrasonic thickness surveys, shear-wave weld examination and radiography. South and west of the city, Port Fourchon functions as the onshore logistics base for the large majority of Gulf of Mexico deepwater oil and gas production — subsea trees, risers, platform modules and supply vessels moving through it all carry inspection requirements before deployment and after recovery. The Louisiana Offshore Oil Port, the only US deepwater terminal able to receive a fully loaded supertanker without lightering, sits offshore from the same corridor. Closer to the city, the Port of New Orleans and the marine fabrication and repair yards along the lower Mississippi examine hull structure, cranes and heavy steel to ABS and USCG survey requirements, where magnetic particle carries most of the volume on fatigue-critical welds.

Layered across all of it is the coastal climate: prolonged humidity, salt-laden air and hurricane exposure that together accelerate corrosion under insulation on piping and vessels, and atmospheric corrosion on unlagged steel. That is a genuine, measurable driver of inspection frequency in this specific region, not a generic Gulf Coast talking point, and it is one reason experienced Louisiana inspectors are valued for judgment about where to look, not only for a certificate that says they are allowed to. Atlantis runs this same on-site, follow-the-work model across other [Gulf Coast and national training locations](/training-usa), because the logic — go to the crew rather than make the crew travel — does not change with geography.

Louisiana's LNG build-out downriver in Plaquemines Parish and along the western part of the state adds a further, distinct source of demand: new-construction inspection on liquefaction trains and cryogenic piping calls for radiography and phased array on welds that will operate at temperatures far below anything a typical refinery unit sees, which is a different qualification emphasis than a turnaround crew doing routine thickness surveys. A New Orleans-based technician who wants to work that scope needs method qualification that specifically covers the applicable code — usually ASME Section VIII and B31.3 with project-specific procedure qualification — rather than assuming a general Level II covers it automatically.

sections.heading: Corporate cohorts versus individual enrollment — what actually changes
paragraphs: The practical differences between an employer-sponsored cohort and an individual signing up alone go beyond who pays. A corporate cohort is scheduled around the client's own production calendar — often built to land before a turnaround window rather than on a fixed public calendar — and it trains against the employer's own Written Practice from day one, using the employer's own equipment models and, where possible, specimens that resemble what the crew will actually examine in production. Every technician in the cohort finishes with a personnel file built the same way: same procedures, same Level III administering the exams, same documentation format. That consistency is what a client audit is actually looking for when it reviews a contractor's technician roster — not that certificates exist, but that they were issued under one coherent, defensible process rather than assembled from whatever each technician happened to bring from a previous employer.

An individual enrolling alone does not get that head start. Training can be completed through a scheduled cohort or blended delivery, but the certificate itself still has to be issued by an employer against that employer's Written Practice — SNT-TC-1A does not permit a training provider to certify someone into a vacuum. That means the practical bottleneck for an individual is rarely the training itself; it is finding the employer relationship that will certify against documented on-the-job hours once training is complete. Candidates who line up an employer first and training second generally reach a working Level II certificate faster than candidates who train first and look for work afterward, simply because the experience clock cannot start until the employment does. For a crew with a turnaround date already on the calendar, the useful next step is a direct conversation about [scheduling a cohort](/contact) rather than a generic quote request.

Procurement looks different too. A corporate cohort is typically arranged well ahead of a turnaround window and locked into a training and outage schedule set months in advance, while an individual candidate typically enrolls into whatever cohort or blended slot is next available. Neither path is a shortcut around the underlying experience requirement, but a company sending a full crew through the same cohort captures a second benefit an individual cannot: the Level III running the exams already knows the plant's own procedures and equipment, so specific and practical exam content is built around exactly what the crew will be examining on Monday morning rather than a generic industry scenario.

facets.q: What passing grade does SNT-TC-1A recommend for a Level II examination?
facets.a: SNT-TC-1A recommends a minimum of 70% on the general examination, 70% on the specific examination, and 80% on the practical examination, with an 80% composite average required across all three. An employer's Written Practice can raise those thresholds — some Gulf Coast operators require a higher composite for methods tied to fitness-for-service decisions — but SNT-TC-1A discourages setting them lower, since the recommended grades already represent a floor rather than a target.

facets.q: How often does a Level II certificate need to be renewed?
facets.a: SNT-TC-1A leaves the exact interval to the employer's Written Practice rather than fixing one, but recommends it not exceed five years and requires either reexamination or documented evidence of continued satisfactory performance in the method at renewal. Layered on top of that cycle is an annual near-vision acuity and colour-contrast check that runs independently — a technician can hold a current certificate and still be pulled from interpretation duty on a failed vision test.

facets.q: Why does a coastal climate like New Orleans change inspection frequency?
facets.a: Prolonged humidity, salt-laden air and repeated hurricane exposure accelerate corrosion under insulation on piping and vessels, and atmospheric corrosion on unlagged steel, faster than a code-minimum inspection interval assumes. Operators in this region commonly shorten ultrasonic thickness survey frequency below the API 510 or API 570 code minimum in response to actual measured corrosion rates, not because the code requires it — a judgment that rests on inspection history, not on the certificate alone.

facets.q: Does a corporate cohort still produce individually issued certificates?
facets.a: Yes. Each technician in a cohort is examined and certified individually against the same employer Written Practice — there is no shared or group certificate under SNT-TC-1A. What a cohort standardizes is the process behind those individual certificates: the same Level III administering every exam, the same procedures, equipment and specimens, and the same documentation format, so the resulting personnel records are consistent across the whole crew rather than reflecting whatever each technician's prior employer happened to document.

facets.q: What role does Port Fourchon play in Louisiana's NDE demand?
facets.a: Port Fourchon is the onshore logistics base supporting the large majority of Gulf of Mexico deepwater oil and gas production, so the subsea trees, risers, platform modules and supply vessels staged through it all carry method-level inspection requirements before deployment and again after recovery for repair or requalification. That steady traffic is one reason ultrasonic and magnetic particle demand in this region tracks offshore activity as closely as it tracks refinery turnaround schedules.

answer: Hyderabad's certified-technician demand is driven less by refining turnarounds and more by manufacturing: nuclear fuel component production, heavy castings and forgings for power equipment, defense ordnance fabrication, and pharmaceutical vessel construction. Training here weights radiography and eddy current testing for tube and weld inspection alongside the core UT, MT and PT methods, since the city has no offshore or marine inspection work to draw technicians toward.
expansion: Telangana is landlocked, so Hyderabad's NDT market never developed the offshore or topside marine specialization that shapes hiring in coastal Indian cities — instead it grew around government-linked heavy engineering and manufacturing: a nuclear fuel fabrication complex, a large power-equipment castings and forgings works, defense ordnance production, and a dense pharmaceutical and bulk-drug manufacturing base. Each pulls a different method mix toward the front of a training plan. A written practice under SNT-TC-1A governs what any of that certification actually means in practice — naming qualification requirements, experience-hour minimums, examination content and recertification intervals — and corporate cohorts trained against a client's own written practice produce a different examination and paper trail than individual enrollment against a portable scheme. Employers and auditors here check the written practice and the experience-hour log behind a certificate, not the wallet card alone, and government or PSU-linked buyers typically go one step further and verify the training provider's own instructor credentials.
source: ASNT SNT-TC-1A

sections.heading: Hyderabad's industrial base: what actually pulls NDT technicians into this market
paragraphs: Telangana is landlocked, so this market draws none of the offshore or topside marine inspection work that shapes hiring and method emphasis in coastal Indian NDT hubs — the pull here is manufacturing and government-linked heavy engineering instead. The Nuclear Fuel Complex, a Department of Atomic Energy unit based in Hyderabad, fabricates zirconium-alloy fuel assemblies for India's nuclear power reactors, and cladding-tube integrity on that work is checked almost entirely by eddy current testing and ultrasonic testing under DAE quality procedures — a method emphasis rarely seen in a refinery-driven training market and one that rewards a technician who has gone deep on tube inspection rather than broad across every method. That depth matters in practice: thin-wall zirconium-alloy tube calls for bobbin-coil, often multi-frequency eddy current technique tuned to a specific tube geometry and alloy response, which a general Level II eddy current course rarely drills to the level a fuel-fabrication inspection actually needs.

Heavy engineering adds a second, larger pull: BHEL's Ramachandrapuram works near Hyderabad produces heat exchangers, industrial valves, and large castings and forgings for the power and process sector, generating steady demand for radiographic and ultrasonic testing on pressure-retaining welds and for magnetic particle and liquid penetrant testing on cast and forged components before and after machining. Casting inspection in particular runs to its own acceptance logic — radiographic sensitivity requirements under ASTM E94/E1032 or the equivalent ASME casting-quality standards are stricter and the defect vocabulary (shrinkage, porosity, cold shut, inclusions) is different from the weld-defect vocabulary a technician trained purely on piping and pressure-vessel welds already knows, so a Hyderabad training plan has to cover both. Defense-sector manufacturing — Bharat Dynamics Limited is headquartered in Hyderabad, alongside DRDO-linked propulsion and ordnance development work in the city — adds radiography-heavy demand of a different character again, examining propellant grain integrity, solid-motor casings, and structural welds against client-written specifications rather than a public code, which is its own discipline for a technician to pick up.

Pharmaceutical and bulk-drug manufacturing is Hyderabad's other major driver, and it is easy to underweight in an NDT training plan because the demand pattern looks different from a refinery's. Process vessels and reactors here are typically new-build ASME Section VIII or IBR-code equipment, fabricated and examined once at construction rather than re-inspected on a recurring in-service interval — which pulls the sector's NDT demand toward fabrication-stage radiography and ultrasonic testing rather than the periodic corrosion-monitoring work that dominates a refining town's training needs.

sections.heading: The written practice, and what Level I to II to III actually requires
paragraphs: Under SNT-TC-1A, every employer maintains a written practice — a document, not a certificate — naming the methods it certifies personnel in, the qualification requirements for each level, the training-hour and experience-hour minimums, the examination content and passing scores, vision-test intervals, and recertification periods. A technician's certification is only ever as good as the written practice it was issued against, which is why an experienced auditor asks to see the [written practice](/asnt-certification) before they look at the wallet card — the card alone proves nothing about what standard the holder was actually measured against.

Level I performs specific calibrations and examinations to written instructions under Level II or III supervision, and becomes eligible only after both training hours and a documented minimum of on-the-job experience hours in that method. Level II interprets and evaluates results against the applicable code and signs the report other people rely on — the level most fabrication and heavy-engineering contracts in Hyderabad name explicitly, for exactly that reason. Level III writes and approves the procedures Level I and II staff work to, administers or oversees the practical and general examinations, and typically holds ASNT central certification or an equivalent that the employer's own written practice is built around. The examination structure itself is three-part at every level — a general exam on method fundamentals, a specific exam on the procedures and equipment the employer actually uses, and a practical exam on real or representative specimens — and a candidate can pass the general and specific sections cleanly and still be held back on the practical if their hands-on technique does not match what the written practice requires.

Vision testing is a harder gate than most candidates expect going in: near-vision acuity — commonly Jaeger 1 or an equivalent standard — and a color-contrast check, both repeated at least annually, sit outside the technical exam entirely but block certification at every level regardless of exam score. Given how radiography-heavy Hyderabad's defense and heavy-engineering work runs, this is a filter worth clearing early rather than discovering after a candidate has already invested weeks in method training.

sections.heading: Corporate cohorts versus individual enrollment — where the model actually diverges
paragraphs: A corporate cohort trains against the client's own written practice, not a generic one, and that single fact reshapes the whole programme. The practical examination is built on the client's actual specimens — a casting geometry from a heavy-engineering shop, a pharma vessel weld coupon, a specific tube configuration — rather than standardized training blocks, and the client's own Level III typically signs the certification, or Atlantis's Level III signs under a written practice the client has reviewed and adopted. Either way, the audit trail a client's quality department or an outside auditor will eventually pull is generated during training itself, not assembled afterward from scattered records.

Individual enrollment runs against a scheme built to travel between employers instead: ASNT SNT-TC-1A employer-based routes or ISO 9712 central certification, prepared through scheduled cohorts or blended online-theory-plus-supervised-practical delivery, so a technician not yet attached to a specific employer's written practice still leaves with a credential the next employer can build a review on rather than start from nothing. Where a candidate wants that credential backed by ongoing procedure and Level III support rather than a one-time exam, [outsourced Level III oversight](/consulting/asnt-level-iii-consulting-services) is the piece that carries past the training itself.

The two models also diverge on scheduling logic. Corporate cohorts sequence around a shift pattern or a planned shutdown window so the crew keeps producing while it qualifies; individual cohorts run to a fixed calendar because there is no single production schedule to protect. Neither model substitutes for the other — a company building out an in-house inspection function in Hyderabad typically needs both, corporate delivery for the standing crew and an individual pathway for new hires brought on between cohort cycles.

One more divergence is specific to Hyderabad's defense- and DRDO-adjacent employer base: where the client's specifications or specimen geometry are themselves controlled or proprietary, a corporate cohort has to be scoped and documented differently from the start — training material, specimens and even attendance records get handled under the client's own information-control rules rather than a standard curriculum, which is a planning conversation Atlantis has before the cohort is scheduled, not something retrofitted afterward.

sections.heading: What Hyderabad employers and auditors actually check before they accept a certification
paragraphs: A credentialing file gets checked, not just a wallet card. What a client's inspection department, an ISO 9001 auditor, or — for radiography specifically — AERB actually pulls is the written practice the certificate was issued against, the signing Level III's own current certification, the logged and supervisor-countersigned experience-hour record, the vision-test date, and the examination scores on file. A certificate with no traceable written practice behind it gets treated as unverifiable, which in an audit is worse than a weak score on record.

Recertification intervals matter as much as the original exam did: SNT-TC-1A-based certifications typically run three to five years depending on what the employer's written practice specifies, ISO 9712 runs on its own defined cycle, and radiography personnel in India additionally answer to AERB's separate licensing renewal — a government-administered process layered on top of the NDT certification, not a replacement for it. A technician holding an expired AERB license and a current NDT certificate is still not authorized to operate a radiation source, and Hyderabad's inspection managers check both dates independently for that reason. Some of the underlying method and terminology references worth keeping on hand for that kind of check sit at Atlantis's [standards reference](/standards).

Technicians targeting Hyderabad's government and PSU-linked employers specifically run into one more check that generic private-sector hiring rarely applies: whether the training provider itself can be named and its Level III's credentials verified independently, since these organizations' own quality systems require traceability all the way back to who delivered the training, not just who received it. It is part of why Atlantis documents instructor credentials as a standard part of the training record handed over at the close of a cohort — a detail worth raising directly when you [scope a Hyderabad programme](/contact).

facets.q: Does Hyderabad NDT training cover offshore or marine inspection methods?
facets.a: No — Telangana is landlocked, so Hyderabad cohorts do not include ROV-based ultrasonic testing, cathodic protection surveys, or other offshore-specific work. Training here instead weights radiography, eddy current testing, and ultrasonic testing for tube and weld inspection in manufacturing, nuclear-fuel, and heavy-engineering settings.

facets.q: How long does it typically take a technician to reach Level II in this market?
facets.a: It depends on prior experience hours far more than classroom time — SNT-TC-1A requires both training hours and a documented minimum of supervised on-the-job experience per method before Level II eligibility, so someone already working under a Level II or III at a fabrication shop generally qualifies faster than someone starting cold.

facets.q: Can a technician certified under one employer's written practice move to another company?
facets.a: Not automatically. SNT-TC-1A certification is employer-based, so a new employer must review and formally accept the written practice a technician was certified against, or requalify them under its own — which is why technicians who expect to change employers often pursue ISO 9712 central certification instead, since it travels without that review step.

facets.q: Does an AERB radiography license replace ASNT or ISO 9712 certification?
facets.a: No — AERB's Radiation Safety Officer and Radiographer licensing under India's atomic-energy regulation runs alongside NDT certification, not in place of it. A radiography technician in Hyderabad generally needs the NDT certification to perform and interpret the examination and the AERB license to legally operate the radiation source at all.

facets.q: What kind of experience actually counts toward Level I and Level II hours?
facets.a: Only documented, supervised experience in the specific method being certified counts — hours spent on calibrations, setups, and examinations performed under a qualified Level II or III and logged with a supervisor's countersignature. Unsupervised practice, or experience in an adjacent but different method, does not credit toward a written practice's experience-hour minimum.

answer: Certification alone doesn't clear a Hazira operator's audit: client QA also checks that a technician's logged experience hours match the specific method and level claimed, that the annual near-vision and color-perception test is current, and that the sponsoring Level III's own certificate is traceable. Corporate cohorts assemble that record trail during training rather than after it.
expansion: Surat's inspection demand runs through a compact industrial belt, but the certification question a technician or employer actually faces is procedural, not geographic: whose written practice governs the qualification, how progression from Level I through Level III is documented, and what a client's inspection department checks before it accepts the paperwork. SNT-TC-1A leaves training-hour minimums, experience-hour minimums, and the recertification interval to the employer's own written practice rather than a single fixed rulebook, which is why two Level II ultrasonic technicians certified a few kilometres apart at Hazira can carry qualifications that aren't automatically interchangeable between employers. ISO 9712, administered by an accredited third-party certification body rather than an employer, sidesteps that portability problem and is increasingly the scheme export-facing fabrication contracts specify. Both routes lead to a real, auditable qualification — the difference is who stands behind the paperwork when a client's QA team asks to see it.
source: ASNT SNT-TC-1A

sections.heading: The written practice behind the Level I to II to III progression
paragraphs: Every SNT-TC-1A programme runs on a document called the written practice, and it's worth understanding what that actually is: not a certificate, but the employer's own internal standard describing which methods and levels it qualifies personnel in, the minimum classroom and on-the-job hours required for each, the vision-test requirements, and how examinations are administered. A candidate sits three distinct exams per method — a general exam on NDT theory common to the method, a specific exam on the codes, procedures, and equipment the employer actually uses, and a practical exam demonstrating the technique on real or representative specimens under observation. Level II adds a procedure-interpretation and reporting component; there's no shortcut past the practical regardless of how strong the written scores are.

Progression between levels is hours-plus-experience, not tenure. Moving from Level I to Level II requires additional documented training hours and a minimum period of verified on-the-job experience performing that specific method under supervision, logged and signed off, not assumed from time employed. Vision is checked at intake with a near-vision acuity test and, for methods where indications are colour-coded such as magnetic particle and liquid penetrant testing, a colour-perception test, then re-verified annually; a missed or failed retest suspends the certification regardless of exam history. Recertification runs on an interval the written practice sets, commonly every three to five years, and typically requires either re-examination or documented evidence of continued satisfactory performance in the method, reviewed and signed by the approving Level III.

Level III itself has two legitimate routes worth knowing apart. An employer-qualified Level III meets the written practice's own training and experience requirements as documented and approved internally, valid for that employer's scope of work. An ASNT NDT Level III Certificate holder is centrally certified by ASNT itself, having passed ASNT's Basic, Method, and Specific examinations independent of any one employer, which is why the credential travels between employers and is often what an outside client or auditor wants to see behind a written practice's approval signature. Programmes that need that outside sign-off, or a written practice built and defended well enough to hold up under a client audit, typically bring in [outsourced Level III oversight](/consulting/asnt-level-iii-consulting-services) rather than try to build the function from a standing start.

sections.heading: What a Hazira client auditor actually checks before accepting a certificate
paragraphs: A certificate on its own rarely satisfies a client inspection department at Hazira; what actually gets checked is the paper trail sitting behind it. First is traceability: does the written practice reference a recognised [standard](/standards), SNT-TC-1A or ISO 9712, and is it dated, version-controlled, and approved by a named, currently-certified Level III, rather than referenced generically as if any written practice will do. Second is the experience-hour log itself: hours have to match the specific method and level being claimed, and an auditor reviewing a Level II ultrasonic claim will ask to see UT-specific hours, not a generic combined NDT experience total across every method a technician has touched.

Third is currency. A lapsed vision retest or a certification past its recertification date is treated as no certification at all, however strong the original exam scores were — this is the single most common finding in a personnel-qualification audit, because it's a date sitting quietly on a form rather than a visible skill gap, and it's easy to miss if records aren't tracked centrally across a crew. Fourth, the auditor traces the approving Level III's own signature back to a currently valid certification carrying the right scope: a Level III approved for ultrasonic and radiographic testing cannot validly sign off a penetrant testing qualification, no matter how experienced they are in general terms.

Fifth, for contracts that specify ISO 9712 rather than SNT-TC-1A, common on export fabrication and EPC-driven work out of Hazira, the auditor can usually verify the certificate directly against the issuing accredited certification body's own registry, which is the practical reason some clients prefer it: it doesn't depend on trusting one employer's internal written practice, it depends on a third party's public record instead. That independence is also why ISO 9712 tends to travel more cleanly between employers than an employer-qualified SNT-TC-1A credential does, even though both remain legitimate, code-recognised routes into the same inspection work. The [NDT glossary](/glossary) covers how these scheme terms get used and occasionally confused in practice.

sections.heading: Corporate cohorts versus individual enrollment near Hazira
paragraphs: The practical difference isn't only where the training happens. In a corporate cohort, candidates train and certify against the client's own written practice: the client's acceptance criteria, the client's approved procedures, and the client's approving Level III, or a Level III engaged under a service agreement, signing off the qualification. That means the certificate is immediately valid for that employer's actual scope of work the day training ends, with no gap between what was tested and what the technician will be asked to inspect the following week. An individual enrolling independently instead trains toward a general SNT-TC-1A or ISO 9712 pathway and then has to have that qualification accepted, method by method, by whichever employer eventually hires them.

Equipment continuity compounds that gap further. Corporate cohorts train on the client's actual instruments, probes, couplant, and reference blocks, so the practical exam and the shop floor are effectively the same equipment, with no re-familiarisation period needed after certifying. A candidate certifying independently trains on generic instructional equipment and specimens instead, which is a perfectly valid qualification on its own terms, but usually still needs a short site-specific orientation before an employer deploys them on a live job, particularly for phased array or automated eddy current setups where every instrument's software and calibration files differ from one facility to the next.

Scheduling and paperwork follow the same split. Corporate programmes are built around a facility's own shift pattern and, for a refinery or petrochemical client, timed deliberately to land before a turnaround window rather than during one, so crews are already qualified and available the moment the outage starts rather than partway through it. At the end, the client receives a complete personnel-qualification file per technician: training hours, experience log, exam scores, current vision test, Level III approval, assembled and ready to hand to a client or third-party auditor. An individual candidate receives the same categories of record but carries the ongoing responsibility of keeping and presenting them to each new employer personally.

sections.heading: Why PAUT and TOFD are gaining ground over radiography at Hazira
paragraphs: Radiographic testing needs a controlled exclusion zone around every shot, and that is genuinely harder to hold in a compact, continuously-operating industrial belt where a petrochemical complex, a gas processing terminal, a steel works, a heavy-engineering yard, and an LNG facility all sit within a few kilometres of shared roads and a dense resident workforce. RT crews working at Hazira routinely plan around night-shift exposure windows and coordinated area clearances precisely because of that density, and that coordination adds real schedule risk on a turnaround with a fixed, non-negotiable outage window.
